lesson.title: What a Circuit Is Actually Saying
lesson.summary: A signal is a voltage or current that varies over time to carry information, the basic quantity every amplifier, filter, and converter in a circuit is built to process rather than simply deliver as power.
lesson.body:
Earlier chapters treated voltage and current mostly as fixed quantities to be solved for: apply Ohm's law, KVL, and KCL to a circuit with given source values, and out comes a specific number of volts or amps at each node and branch. A signal is built from those same physical quantities, voltage or current, but viewed differently: as a function of time, written v(t) or i(t), whose changing shape is what carries meaning. A microphone's output voltage tracing the rise and fall of sound pressure, a temperature sensor's voltage tracking degrees over the course of a day, a digital data line's voltage switching between levels to encode ones and zeros: in each case, the interesting content is not any single voltage value but how that voltage changes.

A simple example makes the distinction concrete. A 9 V battery connected directly to a circuit provides a constant 9 V; that unchanging value carries essentially no information beyond "there is 9 V here." Now take a temperature sensor calibrated to output 10 mV per degree Celsius above a 0 V reference at 0 degrees C. At a room temperature of 23 degrees C, its output is 10 mV/°C x 23°C = 230 mV. Read that voltage again an hour later and it might read 245 mV, corresponding to 24.5 degrees C. The changing voltage over time is what tells you the temperature changed; a fixed voltage could never do that. That changing v(t) is a signal in the sense this chapter sequence uses the term, while the battery's constant 9 V is not.

Signals get sorted along a few independent axes that later chapters build out one at a time: whether the pattern in time repeats exactly, forever, or never quite repeats (periodic versus aperiodic, covered next); whether the signal can take on any value in a continuous range or is restricted to a small set of discrete levels (analog versus digital); and whether time itself is treated as continuous or as a sequence of discrete sample instants (continuous-time versus discrete-time). Every op-amp circuit examined so far in this sequence processes analog, continuous-time signals.

This framing turns out to explain why the non-idealities covered earlier in this chapter sequence, bandwidth, slew rate, saturation, matter in the first place. None of them is really a statement about a single fixed voltage; each is a statement about how faithfully a circuit can reproduce a signal's shape as it changes over time. An op-amp is not just scaling one number by a gain factor, it is trying to track an entire time-varying waveform without lagging, flattening, or clipping it, which is a substantially harder job than the fixed-voltage circuit analysis covered earlier.
